'''Multidimensional interpolation''' is the process of finding a multivariable function $f(x_1,\cdots,x_m)$ that for a definite set of datapoints $\{(x_{1,i},\cdots,x_{m,i},y_i)\mid i\in [0,n], i \in \mathbb{N}\}$ satisfies $f(x_{1,i},\cdots,x_{m,i})=y_i$.

== Methods ==

=== Grid interpolation ===

If a "grid" of $n^m$ datapoints is known, one on each combination of $n$ nodes in each of the $m$ variables:

$$
\{(x_{1,i_1},\cdots,x_{m,i_m},y_{i_1,\cdots,i_m})\mid i_1,\cdots,i_m \in [0,n-1],\, i_1,\cdots,i_m \in \mathbb{N}\}
$$

then the interpolant is the multivariable Lagrange polynomial

$$
f(x_1,\cdots,x_m)=\sum_{i_1=0}^{n-1}\cdots\sum_{i_m=0}^{n-1}y_{i_1,\cdots,i_m}\prod_{j=1}^{m}L^{(j)}_{i_j}(x_j),\qquad L^{(j)}_{i}(x_j)=\prod_{\substack{k=0\\k\neq i}}^{n-1}\frac{x_j-x_{j,k}}{x_{j,i}-x_{j,k}}
$$

where $L^{(j)}_i$ is the [[Polynomial_interpolation#Lagrange_polynomial|Lagrange basis polynomial]] of the variable $x_j$, built on that variable's $n$ nodes.

Each factor $L^{(j)}_{i_j}(x_j)$ equals one at the node $x_{j,i_j}$ and zero at the other $n-1$ nodes of $x_j$. The product of the $m$ factors is therefore one at the single datapoint $(x_{1,i_1},\cdots,x_{m,i_m})$ and zero at every other datapoint, so each of the $n^m$ terms carries exactly its own reading and vanishes at all the rest, and the sum passes through all $n^m$ datapoints.

The result is the '''tensor product''' interpolant, and it is unique among polynomials of degree at most $n-1$ in each variable: a difference of two of them vanishes at all $n^m$ nodes, and such a difference, read as a polynomial of degree at most $n-1$ in $x_1$, has $n$ roots for every fixed choice of the other variables, so each of its coefficients vanishes at those choices, one variable at a time<ref>{{#cite:Q2392}}</ref>. In the Lagrange basis the coefficients are the readings themselves, so nothing is solved for: the $n^m$ coefficients and the $n^m$ datapoints are the same numbers.

{{Hidden example}}
'''Surface temperature over a square of weather stations.''' Sixteen stations sit on a $4\times4$ grid, spaced $1^\circ$ of longitude apart from west to east and $1^\circ$ of latitude apart from south to north. The readings are synthetic, constructed for this example:

{| class="wikitable"
|+ Temperature ($^\circ$C) at each station
! latitude $\downarrow$ / longitude $\rightarrow$ !! $0^\circ$E !! $1^\circ$E !! $2^\circ$E !! $3^\circ$E
|-
! $53^\circ$N
| 18.4 || 19.1 || 20.6 || 21.8
|-
! $52^\circ$N
| 20.1 || 20.9 || 22.3 || 23.5
|-
! $51^\circ$N
| 21.7 || 22.5 || 23.9 || 25.0
|-
! $50^\circ$N
| 22.8 || 23.6 || 24.9 || 26.1
|}

With $m=2$ and $n=4$ the sum has $n^m=16$ terms, one per station. Number the longitude nodes $x_{1,1}=0$, $x_{1,2}=1$, $x_{1,3}=2$, $x_{1,4}=3$ and the latitude nodes $x_{2,1}=50$, $x_{2,2}=51$, $x_{2,3}=52$, $x_{2,4}=53$, so that $i_1=1$ is the column at $0^\circ$E and $i_2=1$ the row at $50^\circ$N, the bottom row of the table:

$$
f(x_1,x_2)=\sum_{i_1=1}^{4}\sum_{i_2=1}^{4}y_{i_1,i_2}\,L_{1i_1}(x_1)\,L_{2i_2}(x_2)
$$

where $y_{i_1,i_2}$ is the reading in column $i_1$ and row $i_2$, and $L_{ji_j}$ is the general $L^{(j)}_{i_j}$ with the node index counted from $1$ rather than from $0$.

'''The eight basis polynomials.''' Four are built on the longitude nodes $0,1,2,3$ and are functions of $x_1$; four are built on the latitude nodes $50,51,52,53$ and are functions of $x_2$:

$$
L_{11}(x_1)=-\frac{(x_1-1)(x_1-2)(x_1-3)}{6}=-\frac{1}{6}x_1^3+x_1^2-\frac{11}{6}x_1+1,\qquad L_{12}(x_1)=\frac{x_1(x_1-2)(x_1-3)}{2}=\frac{1}{2}x_1^3-\frac{5}{2}x_1^2+3x_1
$$

$$
L_{13}(x_1)=-\frac{x_1(x_1-1)(x_1-3)}{2}=-\frac{1}{2}x_1^3+2x_1^2-\frac{3}{2}x_1,\qquad L_{14}(x_1)=\frac{x_1(x_1-1)(x_1-2)}{6}=\frac{1}{6}x_1^3-\frac{1}{2}x_1^2+\frac{1}{3}x_1
$$

$$
L_{21}(x_2)=-\frac{(x_2-51)(x_2-52)(x_2-53)}{6}=-\frac{1}{6}x_2^3+26x_2^2-\frac{8111}{6}x_2+23426,\qquad L_{22}(x_2)=\frac{(x_2-50)(x_2-52)(x_2-53)}{2}=\frac{1}{2}x_2^3-\frac{155}{2}x_2^2+4003x_2-68900
$$

$$
L_{23}(x_2)=-\frac{(x_2-50)(x_2-51)(x_2-53)}{2}=-\frac{1}{2}x_2^3+77x_2^2-\frac{7903}{2}x_2+67575,\qquad L_{24}(x_2)=\frac{(x_2-50)(x_2-51)(x_2-52)}{6}=\frac{1}{6}x_2^3-\frac{51}{2}x_2^2+\frac{3901}{3}x_2-22100
$$

'''The polynomial, developed along each parallel.''' Collecting the terms of one latitude row turns $f$ into a cubic in $x_1$ whose four coefficients are the $x_2$ polynomials:

$$
f(x_1,x_2)=Q_1(x_1)L_{21}(x_2)+Q_2(x_1)L_{22}(x_2)+Q_3(x_1)L_{23}(x_2)+Q_4(x_1)L_{24}(x_2),\qquad Q_{i_2}(x_1)=\sum_{i_1=1}^{4}y_{i_1,i_2}L_{1i_1}(x_1)
$$

so $Q_{i_2}$ is the cubic through the four readings of the parallel at $x_{2,i_2}$. Carrying out the four sums:

$$
Q_1(x_1)=-\frac{1}{10}x_1^3+\frac{11}{20}x_1^2+\frac{7}{20}x_1+\frac{114}{5}\ \ (50^\circ\mathrm{N}),\qquad Q_2(x_1)=-\frac{3}{20}x_1^3+\frac{3}{4}x_1^2+\frac{1}{5}x_1+\frac{217}{10}\ \ (51^\circ\mathrm{N})
$$

$$
Q_3(x_1)=-\frac{2}{15}x_1^3+\frac{7}{10}x_1^2+\frac{7}{30}x_1+\frac{201}{10}\ \ (52^\circ\mathrm{N}),\qquad Q_4(x_1)=-\frac{11}{60}x_1^3+\frac{19}{20}x_1^2-\frac{1}{15}x_1+\frac{92}{5}\ \ (53^\circ\mathrm{N})
$$

Each constant term is that parallel's reading at $0^\circ$E, as it must be.

'''The polynomial in $x_1$ and $x_2$.''' With every factor written out, the interpolant is

$$
f(x_1,x_2)=\left(-\frac{1}{10}x_1^3+\frac{11}{20}x_1^2+\frac{7}{20}x_1+\frac{114}{5}\right)\left(-\frac{(x_2-51)(x_2-52)(x_2-53)}{6}\right)
$$

$$
{}+\left(-\frac{3}{20}x_1^3+\frac{3}{4}x_1^2+\frac{1}{5}x_1+\frac{217}{10}\right)\frac{(x_2-50)(x_2-52)(x_2-53)}{2}
$$

$$
{}+\left(-\frac{2}{15}x_1^3+\frac{7}{10}x_1^2+\frac{7}{30}x_1+\frac{201}{10}\right)\left(-\frac{(x_2-50)(x_2-51)(x_2-53)}{2}\right)
$$

$$
{}+\left(-\frac{11}{60}x_1^3+\frac{19}{20}x_1^2-\frac{1}{15}x_1+\frac{92}{5}\right)\frac{(x_2-50)(x_2-51)(x_2-52)}{6}
$$

Multiplied out, it has 16 terms and degree at most 3 in each variable; the large coefficients come from the latitude nodes sitting at 50 to 53 rather than at 0 to 3:

$$
f(x_1,x_2)=-\tfrac{1}{45}x_1^3x_2^3+\tfrac{103}{30}x_1^3x_2^2-\tfrac{31823}{180}x_1^3x_2+\tfrac{45511}{15}x_1^3+\tfrac{11}{120}x_1^2x_2^3-\tfrac{283}{20}x_1^2x_2^2+\tfrac{87361}{120}x_1^2x_2-\tfrac{62416}{5}x_1^2
$$

$$
{}-\tfrac{31}{360}x_1x_2^3+\tfrac{199}{15}x_1x_2^2-\tfrac{245249}{360}x_1x_2+\tfrac{174899}{15}x_1+\tfrac{1}{15}x_2^3-\tfrac{209}{20}x_2^2+\tfrac{32657}{60}x_2-\tfrac{93997}{10}
$$

'''Evaluating at $1.4^\circ$E, $51.6^\circ$N.''' Substitute the point into the polynomial, one variable at a time. The longitude argument first: $x_1=1.4$ needs the four $x_1$ polynomials at that one argument. For instance

$$
L_{12}(1.4)=\frac{1.4\,(1.4-2)(1.4-3)}{(1-0)(1-2)(1-3)}=\frac{1.4\cdot(-0.6)\cdot(-1.6)}{1\cdot(-1)\cdot(-2)}=\frac{1.344}{2}=0.672
$$

and the four of them, beside the four $x_2$ polynomials at the latitude of the query point, are

{| class="wikitable"
|+ The basis polynomials at the two arguments
! $i$ !! $L_{1i}(1.4)$ !! $L_{2i}(51.6)$
|-
! 1
| $-0.064$ || $-0.056$
|-
! 2
| $0.672$ || $0.448$
|-
! 3
| $0.448$ || $0.672$
|-
! 4
| $-0.056$ || $-0.064$
|}

Each column sums to $1$, as it must, since the basis reproduces a constant exactly. Substituting the first column into the four parallels gives the values on the parallels at $1.4^\circ$E. For the row at $50^\circ$N the expanded form and the basis values agree:

$$
Q_1(1.4)=-\tfrac{1}{10}(2.744)+\tfrac{11}{20}(1.96)+\tfrac{7}{20}(1.4)+22.8=-0.2744+1.078+0.49+22.8=24.0936
$$

$$
Q_1(1.4)=-0.064\cdot22.8+0.672\cdot23.6+0.448\cdot24.9-0.056\cdot26.1=24.0936
$$

and the basis values are the quicker route for the other three rows:

$$
Q_2(1.4)=-0.064\cdot21.7+0.672\cdot22.5+0.448\cdot23.9-0.056\cdot25.0=23.0384
$$

$$
Q_3(1.4)=-0.064\cdot20.1+0.672\cdot20.9+0.448\cdot22.3-0.056\cdot23.5=21.4328
$$

$$
Q_4(1.4)=-0.064\cdot18.4+0.672\cdot19.1+0.448\cdot20.6-0.056\cdot21.8=19.6656
$$

The latitude argument is $x_2=51.6$, whose four values are the second column above; for instance

$$
L_{22}(51.6)=\frac{(51.6-50)(51.6-52)(51.6-53)}{(51-50)(51-52)(51-53)}=\frac{1.6\cdot(-0.4)\cdot(-1.4)}{1\cdot(-1)\cdot(-2)}=\frac{0.896}{2}=0.448
$$

Substituting both columns into the polynomial:

$$
f(1.4,51.6)=24.0936(-0.056)+23.0384(0.448)+21.4328(0.672)+19.6656(-0.064)=22.1162
$$

The same arithmetic in code:

<syntaxhighlight lang="python" copy>
import numpy as np

def lagrange_basis(nodes):
    """Lagrange basis polynomials on `nodes`, as coefficient vectors, highest power first."""
    basis = []
    for i in nodes:
        p = np.array([1.0])
        for k in nodes:
            if k != i:
                p = np.polymul(p, [1.0, -k]) / (i - k)
        basis.append(p)
    return basis

def basis_at(basis, x):
    """The basis polynomials evaluated at x."""
    return np.array([np.polyval(p, x) for p in basis])

longitude = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0])           # nodes of x1
latitude = np.array([50.0, 51.0, 52.0, 53.0])        # nodes of x2
L1 = lagrange_basis(longitude)                      # L11 .. L14
L2 = lagrange_basis(latitude)                       # L21 .. L24

temperature = np.array([[22.8, 23.6, 24.9, 26.1],
                        [21.7, 22.5, 23.9, 25.0],
                        [20.1, 20.9, 22.3, 23.5],
                        [18.4, 19.1, 20.6, 21.8]])   # row = latitude 50, 51, 52, 53; column = longitude 0, 1, 2, 3

print(np.round(L1, 4))                               # L11 .. L14, highest power first
print(np.round(L2, 4))                               # L21 .. L24, highest power first
print(np.round(temperature @ np.array(L1), 4))       # Q1 .. Q4, row by row
print(basis_at(L1, 1.4))                             # [-0.064  0.672  0.448 -0.056]
print(basis_at(L2, 51.6))                            # [-0.056  0.448  0.672 -0.064]

parallel = temperature @ basis_at(L1, 1.4)           # Q1 .. Q4 at 1.4 E
print(parallel)                                      # [24.0936 23.0384 21.4328 19.6656]
print(parallel @ basis_at(L2, 51.6))                 # 22.1162048
</syntaxhighlight>

Plotting the whole surface only needs the same basis evaluated on a mesh of arguments:

<syntaxhighlight lang="python" copy>
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

lon_plot = np.linspace(0.0, 3.0, 121)
lat_plot = np.linspace(50.0, 53.0, 121)
surface = np.array([[basis_at(L2, y) @ temperature @ basis_at(L1, x)
                     for x in lon_plot] for y in lat_plot])

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9.0, 6.8))
ax = fig.add_subplot(111, projection="3d")
ax.set_box_aspect((1.35, 1.0, 0.62))
mesh_lon, mesh_lat = np.meshgrid(lon_plot, lat_plot)
surf = ax.plot_surface(mesh_lon, mesh_lat, surface, cmap="RdYlBu_r", linewidth=0,
                       antialiased=True, rstride=2, cstride=2, alpha=0.92)
ax.scatter(np.tile(longitude, 4), np.repeat(latitude, 4), temperature.ravel(),
           s=70, color="#c0392b", edgecolor="black", linewidth=0.9,
           depthshade=False, label="16 weather stations")
ax.scatter([1.4], [51.6], [22.116], s=170, color="black", marker="X",
           depthshade=False, label=r"query point (1.4$^\circ$E, 51.6$^\circ$N)")
ax.set_xlabel(r"longitude ($^\circ$E)", labelpad=10)
ax.set_ylabel(r"latitude ($^\circ$N)", labelpad=10)
ax.set_zlabel(r"temperature ($^\circ$C)", labelpad=8)
ax.set_xticks(longitude)
ax.set_yticks(latitude)
ax.set_zlim(16.5, 26.5)
ax.view_init(elev=34, azim=-56)
fig.colorbar(surf, shrink=0.55, pad=0.10, aspect=24,
             label=r"interpolated temperature ($^\circ$C)")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", frameon=False, fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
</syntaxhighlight>

[[File:Bicubic grid interpolation temperature.png|thumb|none|560px|alt=Three-dimensional plot of a gently curving temperature surface over a longitude-latitude grid, with the sixteen station readings marked as red dots and one query point marked with a cross|The interpolating surface through the sixteen station readings, the tensor product of four longitude and four latitude basis polynomials. The query point at $1.4^\circ$E, $51.6^\circ$N is marked with a cross.]]

The temperature falls from about $26\ ^\circ$C in the south-east to about $18\ ^\circ$C in the north-west, so the surface is dominated by a plane tilted towards the north-west, with a gentler curvature across it.
{{End hidden}}

=== Pointwise interpolation ===

Pointwise interpolation (or '''point evaluation''') asks only for the value of $f$ at one new point $(x_1^*,\cdots,x_m^*)$ inside the data range, without constructing $f$ anywhere else. It uses the same grid of $n^m$ datapoints and the same basis polynomials, but regroups the sum one variable at a time instead of writing out its $n^m$ terms.

In two dimensions, the first pass interpolates along $x_1$ inside each row $x_2=x_{2,i_2}$, at the target $x_1^*$:

$$
y^*_{i_2}=\sum_{i_1=0}^{n-1}L^{(1)}_{i_1}(x_1^*)\,y_{i_1,i_2},\qquad \forall i_2\in [0,n-1], i_2 \in \mathbb{N}
$$

The $n$ intermediate values $y^*_{i_2}$ sit at the coordinates $(x_1^*,x_{2,i_2})$, i.e., on a one-dimensional grid in $x_2$, so a second pass interpolates them at $x_2^*$:

$$
f(x_1^*,x_2^*)=\sum_{i_2=0}^{n-1}L^{(2)}_{i_2}(x_2^*)\,y^*_{i_2}
$$

The first pass costs $n$ one-dimensional interpolations and the second costs $1$. In $m$ dimensions the passes shrink by one variable each time, costing $n^{m-1}, n^{m-2}, \cdots, n^0$:

$$
\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}n^{k}=\frac{n^{m}-1}{n-1}
$$

and the passes are exactly the nested form

$$
f(x_1^*,\cdots,x_m^*)=\sum_{i_m=0}^{n-1}L^{(m)}_{i_m}(x_m^*)\sum_{i_{m-1}=0}^{n-1}L^{(m-1)}_{i_{m-1}}(x_{m-1}^*)\cdots\sum_{i_1=0}^{n-1}L^{(1)}_{i_1}(x_1^*)\,y_{i_1,\cdots,i_m}
$$

Each of those weighted sums costs $n$ multiplications, so the nested passes cost $n(n^{m}-1)/(n-1)$ in all. That is fewer than the $m\,n^m$ multiplications needed to sum the $n^m$ terms of [[#Grid_interpolation|grid interpolation]] term by term, because each pass collapses one variable: the first pass does range over the $n^{m-1}$ combinations of known nodes, as a direct sum does, but afterwards one variable is pinned at the target $x_j^*$ and contributes one position instead of $n$. Nothing is thrown away: the same $n^m$ terms are summed either way, and the two counts answer different questions, the value at one point and the whole surface.

The order of the passes does not matter. Collapsing $x_1$ first and then $x_2$ gives the same result as collapsing $x_2$ first and then $x_1$, because the tensor product sum can be regrouped; every ordering evaluates the same polynomial as [[#Grid_interpolation|grid interpolation]]<ref>{{#cite:Q2391}}</ref>.

{| class="wikitable"
|+ Multiplications at one query point, for $n=4$ nodes per axis
! $m$ !! grid interpolation, direct sum, $m\,n^m$ !! pointwise, nested, $n\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}n^{k}$
|-
! 2
| 32 || 20
|-
! 3
| 192 || 84
|-
! 4
| 1024 || 340
|}

For a general number of variables the passes are most conveniently written as contractions, one per variable:

<syntaxhighlight lang="python" copy>
def grid_interpolate_point(nodes, values, point):
    """Interpolated value at `point` from an n_1 x ... x n_m grid.

    nodes  -- one 1-D array of node coordinates per variable, in the same order
              as the axes of `values`
    values -- m-dimensional array, values[i_1, ..., i_m]
    point  -- the m query coordinates
    """
    data = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    for axis in range(len(nodes) - 1, -1, -1):       # collapse one variable per pass
        w = basis_at(lagrange_basis(nodes[axis]), point[axis])
        data = np.tensordot(data, w, axes=([axis], [0]))
    return float(data)
</syntaxhighlight>

For the station grid, `grid_interpolate_point([np.arange(50.0, 54.0), np.arange(0.0, 4.0)], temperature, [51.6, 1.4])` returns `22.1162048...`, which is the two-pass calculation of the example above: four longitude interpolations give $24.0936$, $23.0384$, $21.4328$, and $19.6656\ ^\circ$C on the rows at $50$, $51$, $52$, and $53^\circ$N, and one latitude interpolation of those four values gives the reading at the query point.

<blockquote>
Because these readings happen to be close to planar, bilinear interpolation of the four stations surrounding the query point gives $22.100\ ^\circ$C, only $0.02\ ^\circ$C away from the grid interpolant. The two are not interchangeable, however: the bilinear interpolant is merely continuous where cells meet, whereas the grid interpolant is a single polynomial and therefore smooth everywhere.
</blockquote>
